whyItExists.short: Images make the web visual, but they must be loaded efficiently and described for users who cannot see them.
whyItExists.problem: A raw img tag with no alt text, no size hints, and no format optimization can break layouts, slow pages, and be completely inaccessible.
whyItExists.solution: The img element with alt, width, height, and loading attributes covers the basics. The picture element with srcset enables responsive images that serve the right size/format per device.
whyItExists.impact: Images account for ~50% of page weight on average. Optimising them is the single biggest performance win for most websites.

explainModes.beginner: img shows a picture. src is the image file path. alt is a text description for people who can't see the image (and for screen readers).
explainModes.simple: img requires src (where the image is) and alt (a text description). Always set width and height to prevent layout shifts. Use loading="lazy" for images below the fold.
explainModes.standard: img is a void element (no closing tag). The alt attribute is required for accessibility — empty alt="" is valid for decorative images. width/height prevent Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). The picture element with source allows serving WebP/AVIF with fallbacks and different crops at different breakpoints.
explainModes.technical: The browser uses the sizes attribute alongside srcset to pick the optimal image source based on the viewport. The loading=lazy attribute defers offscreen image requests. Explicit width/height lets the browser reserve the correct aspect-ratio space before the image loads, preventing CLS — a Core Web Vitals metric. fetchpriority=high signals LCP images to the browser's preload scanner.
explainModes.deepDive: The picture element is a structural container — it never renders itself. The browser evaluates source elements top-to-bottom and selects the first matching media/type condition. AVIF offers ~50% smaller files than WebP but has narrower browser support. The decoding=async attribute offloads JPEG/PNG decoding to a background thread. The figure and figcaption elements semantically associate an image with its caption — the implicit ARIA role is `figure`.

content.text: The **img** element embeds an image. It is a **void element** — it has no closing tag.

content.label: Basic image

content.title: alt text is not optional
content.body: Every img must have an alt attribute. For meaningful images, write a description. For purely decorative images, use alt="" (empty) so screen readers skip it.

items: **width / height** — explicit dimensions to prevent layout shift
**loading="lazy"** — defer loading until the image nears the viewport
**decoding="async"** — decode image off the main thread

content.title: Always include the img fallback inside picture
content.body: The img element inside picture is the universal fallback. It also carries the alt, width, and height for all sources.

content.question: What should the alt attribute contain for a purely decorative image?
content.explanation: alt="" (empty) tells screen readers to skip the image completely. This is correct for decorative images that add no informational content. Never omit the attribute entirely.

content.question: Why should you always set explicit width and height on img?
options: To prevent layout shift while the image loads
content.explanation: Without width/height, the browser doesn't know the image dimensions until it downloads the file, causing layout to jump — this is called Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS), a Core Web Vitals metric.

faq.q: What image format should I use?
faq.a: Use AVIF first (best compression), WebP as fallback, then JPEG for photos or PNG for transparency. Use the picture element to serve AVIF/WebP with a JPEG/PNG fallback.

faq.q: What's the difference between loading=lazy and loading=eager?
faq.a: lazy defers the image request until the user scrolls near it — great for images below the fold. eager (the default) loads the image immediately. Never lazy-load the largest above-the-fold image (your LCP image).

faq.q: Can I use SVG as an img source?
faq.a: Yes. works in all modern browsers. SVG is ideal for logos and icons as it scales without quality loss.

examples: Google Images uses srcset to serve optimised sizes per device
Twitter uses WebP with JPEG fallback for all uploaded images
